title: Braess's paradox
hook: Adding a new road to a network can make every driver's journey slower.
peek: In 1968 a German mathematician showed that a shortcut can slow everyone down, because each driver picks the best route for themselves. Cities have since closed roads and found traffic flowed no worse, sometimes better.
lede: In 1968 the German mathematician Dietrich Braess described a strange result. In a road network where every driver chooses the fastest route for themselves, adding a new link can make the journey slower for everyone. Nobody is foolish. Each driver makes a sensible choice, but together those choices settle into a worse pattern than before. Remove the link, and everyone gets home sooner.

bullets.text: In a standard version, 4,000 drivers split between two routes and each takes 65 minutes. Add a free shortcut joining the two routes and everyone switches to it, crowding the slow stretches. The trip rises to 80 minutes, yet no one gains by switching back.

The paradox is a case of what game theorists call a Nash equilibrium: a state where nobody can do better by changing only their own choice. The equilibrium is not the arrangement that is best for the group.

Seoul removed a busy elevated highway over the Cheonggyecheon stream in the early 2000s and turned the area into a park. Traffic around the city did not get the jam many predicted, and some journeys improved.
The same logic works outside traffic. In 1991 Joel Cohen and Paul Horowitz built a hanging weight held by springs and strings in which cutting one string makes the weight rise, not fall.
